lessons.title: Asynchronous Callback Execution Patterns
lessons.description: Callbacks are functions passed to async operations — they run when the operation completes.

sections.heading: How async callbacks work
paragraphs: A callback is a function you pass to another function to be called later. In async operations, the callback runs after the background work finishes — not when you pass it.
list: The async work happens in the background
When done, the callback is placed on the event queue
The callback runs when the call stack is empty

codeExamples.heading: Async callback timing
explanation: Even with a 0ms delay, the callback runs after the current code finishes.
setTimeout schedules the callback on the event queue, not immediately.
The main thread finishes all synchronous code first.
This proves async callbacks always wait for the call stack to clear.

practice.task: Create 3 setTimeouts with delays of 0ms, 100ms, and 50ms. Log their order and predict the output before running.
hints: The order depends on when each is queued and when the stack is free.
Synchronous code always runs before any async callbacks.

keyTakeaways: Callbacks are functions passed to be called when async work completes.
Even 0ms setTimeout doesn't run immediately — it waits for the call stack to clear.
Async callbacks are placed on the event queue and executed when the thread is free.
This is the foundation of JavaScript's non-blocking execution model.
lessons.challenge: Write code that demonstrates callback execution timing with console.time to measure the actual delay.

lessons.title: Node.js Error-First Callback Conventions
lessons.description: The standard Node.js pattern: callbacks receive an error as the first argument, then the result.

sections.heading: Error-first callbacks
paragraphs: In Node.js, the convention is to pass error-first callbacks: the first argument is always an error (or null on success), and subsequent arguments are the result.
list: If no error: error is null, result contains the data
If error: error is an Error object, result is undefined
Always check if (err) before using the result

codeExamples.heading: Error-first callback pattern
explanation: The callback receives (error, result) — error first.
On success, error is null and result contains the data.
On failure, error is an Error object and result is null.
Always check for errors before using the result.
codeExamples.output:
> File loaded: { data: "hello" }
> Error: File not found

practice.task: Write a simulated async function that fetches a user by ID using the error-first callback pattern. Handle both success and error cases.
hints: Use setTimeout to simulate async work.
If ID doesn't exist, call callback(new Error("Not found"), null).

keyTakeaways: Error-first callbacks put the error as the first argument.
Always check if (err) before accessing the result.
This pattern is the foundation of Node.js async operations.
Modern async/await is preferred, but understanding this pattern is essential for legacy code.
lessons.challenge: Write a simulated database lookup function with error-first callbacks, then refactor it to return a Promise.

lessons.title: Nesting Issues, Inverted Control & Callback Hell
lessons.description: When callbacks nest deeply, code becomes unreadable — this problem is called callback hell.

sections.heading: Callback hell
paragraphs: When multiple async operations depend on each other, callbacks nest inside callbacks. The result is deeply indented, hard to read, and difficult to debug — the infamous "callback hell" or "pyramid of doom."
list: Deep nesting makes code hard to follow
Error handling must be repeated at every level
Inverted control: you give control to the callback and hope it calls you back correctly
Promises and async/await solve this problem

codeExamples.heading: Callback hell vs clean async code
explanation: The callback version nests 3 levels deep — hard to read and maintain.
Error handling is repeated at every level — verbose and error-prone.
The Promise version is flat and readable — each step on its own line.
Promises solve callback hell by chaining async operations.
codeExamples.output:
> Step 1 done
> Step 2 done
> Step 3 done

practice.task: Take a 3-level nested callback and flatten it using Promises. Identify the inversion of control problem in the callback version.
hints: Replace each callback with a .then() chain.
Move error handling to a single .catch() at the end.
Notice how much easier the flat chain is to read.

keyTakeaways: Callback hell occurs when async operations nest deeply.
Inverted control means you hand control to the callback and trust it to work correctly.
Error handling in nested callbacks is repetitive and error-prone.
Promises and async/await were created specifically to solve callback hell.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite a 4-level callback hell example using Promises, then again using async/await.
